newsitem.title: GHANA: Malaysian-led group wins Ghana Telecom stake.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian-led group wins Ghana Telecom stake.

text.p: Ghana said on Wednesday it had awarded a Malaysian-led consortium a 30 percent strategic stake in its state telecom company and had chosen a consortium led by U.S. company Western Wireless to operate a rival network.

Telekom Malaysia Berhad, the latest in a string of Malaysian companies to invest in the gold and cocoa-producing West African nation, and its consortium would also run a privatised Ghana Telcom Limited under the deal.

Transport and Communications Minister Edward Salia told a news conference the two groups had emerged as winners of a privatisation tendering process launched in February. The government opened bids on Monday.

"We believe the offers we received are good and will help us achieve the objectives for our privatisation programme," Salia said. "This will help meet the current backlog of 300,000 telephone lines being demanded by consumers and ensure efficiency and improved services."

Telekom Malaysia and its G-COM consortium with three Ghanaian companies paid $38 million for the 30 percent stake in Ghana Telecom Limited. The government plans to sell a further 21 percent to the public but has not yet made clear how or when.

A consortium of African Communications Group, Western Wireless and Ghana National Petroleum Company emerged as the top bidder for a licence to set up a rival national network of fixed telecommunications services with an offer of $10.1 million.
The idea behind a second nationwide telephone company is to create competition. Ghana is the first country in Africa to go through with this privatisation option in the telecommunications sector.

Western Wireless is a cellular provider in the United States. Based in the U.S. city of Cambridge, African Communications Group has been operating wireless card pay telephones and a pager system in Tanzania since 1993.
"We are very happy that we have won," Monique Maddy, president of African Communications Group, told Reuters on Monday after bids were opened.
Officials for the consortium say it wants to invest between $40 million and $70 million in the coming five years.
In June 1996 Ghana Telecom had about 100,000 telephone lines installed and 6,000 mobile cellular subscribers, according to a memorandum by the Ministry of Tranport and Communications.
In the second half of 1996 government planned to construct 100,000 new lines, raising total availability to 200,000 lines or 1.3 telephone per 100 inhabitants.
In 1994 Ghana Telecom's total revenues amounted to $61 million, against $72 million in 1993. Total operating costs were $42 million against $49 million in 1993.

Net income was $7.105 million in 1994 against $10.490 million in 1993. Value of total assets was $214 million in 1994, including $72 million current assets, against $121 million in 1993, including $67 million current assets.
Total liabilities amounted to $272 million in 1994, including $235 million in long term debt. In 1993, total liabilities amounted to $160 million including $128 million in long-term debt.
